body:
What is netiquette?

Netiquette (network etiquette) means the accepted principles of polite, ethical and responsible conduct when people communicate or share information through the Internet. They apply to email, messaging groups, social media, online classes, discussion forums and other digital spaces. The basic values are familiar from face-to-face life: honesty, courtesy, respect for privacy and consideration for the effects of one's actions.

A digital citizen, also called a netizen, is a person who participates in digital society through Internet-connected technologies. Responsible digital citizenship means using these technologies safely, ethically and with respect for other people's rights.

Netiquette is broader than good grammar or polite greetings. A beautifully worded message may still be irresponsible if it reveals someone's personal information, copies a creator's work without proper credit or spreads an unverified claim. Equally, a person's right to express disagreement does not justify threats or humiliation.

Why online conduct needs care

Online communication can reach many people rapidly, and a message may be forwarded or captured as a screenshot. Written messages often lack the facial expressions and tone that help people understand speech. A joke or criticism may therefore be misinterpreted, particularly in a group with different languages, ages or cultural backgrounds. Digital actions can also leave a digital footprint: a record associated with activity on digital services.

Three complementary duties

  • Be ethical: provide truthful information, acknowledge original creators and avoid presenting others' work as your own.
  • Be respectful: communicate without abuse, recognise diversity and obtain permission before sharing another person's private content.
  • Be responsible: guard personal information, avoid amplifying harm and use digital services in a balanced way.

These are related but not identical. Etiquette concerns appropriate behaviour; privacy concerns control over personal information; and information accuracy concerns whether a claim is supported by evidence. A single act, such as forwarding a private but false message, may fail all 3 tests.

Netiquette principles are behavioural guidance. They should not be confused with a complete statement of legal rights or offences: an action may be discourteous without being unlawful, and some harmful acts may also have legal consequences.

Prelims focus

  • Netiquette means responsible conduct in Internet-based communication.
  • Netizen is another term for a digital citizen.
  • Ethical conduct, respectful communication and responsible sharing are complementary duties.
  • Trap: A polite message is not necessarily an ethical message if it violates privacy or spreads false information.

[NCERT, Computer Science, Class 11, Ch. 11 'Societal Impact', §§11.2–11.3, pp. 230–231, 2026–27 reprint; CBSE and Cyber Peace Foundation, Cyber Safety: Handbook for Students of Secondary and Senior Secondary Schools, 2020, Ch. 5 'Digital Etiquette', p. 29.]

title: Netiquette and Responsible Digital Citizenship

body:
Clear, courteous communication

Respectful online communication addresses the subject without degrading the person. Before sending a message, consider who will read it, the purpose, whether the language could be misunderstood and whether a public group is the appropriate audience. Clear subject lines, relevant details and a neutral tone help the recipient understand the message. Repeated messages demanding an immediate reply may disregard the recipient's time.

Netiquette applies to both synchronous communication, such as a live video call or chat, and asynchronous communication, such as email or a forum post that may be read later. In a video class or meeting, letting others finish, muting unnecessary background noise and not circulating recordings without permission are practical forms of respect. In messages, writing an entire disagreement in capital letters or using insulting expressions can make an exchange appear aggressive.

A student may write, 'I disagree because the official notice gives a different date,' instead of 'Only a fool would believe that date.' The first challenges a claim with a reason; the second attacks a person.

Disagreement, trolling and cyberbullying are different

BehaviourMain featureAppropriate response
Constructive disagreementCriticism of an idea, claim or action without personal abuseDiscuss evidence and remain civil
TrollingDeliberately provocative messages intended to upset others or disrupt discussionAvoid rewarding provocation; use moderation tools when needed
CyberbullyingOnline behaviour that intimidates, humiliates or targets someone, often repeatedlyPreserve evidence, seek support, block or report as appropriate

Cyberbullying can involve repeated insults, rumours, humiliation, threats or posting someone's personal details to harm them. A single rude statement is not automatically the same as a sustained pattern of bullying; nevertheless, one serious threat or harmful disclosure deserves immediate attention. Cyberstalking involves persistent unwanted online pursuit or monitoring; it should not be treated as ordinary disagreement.

Responding without making harm worse

If a comment is merely critical, a factual and calm reply may settle the disagreement. If someone is deliberately provoking a quarrel, a prolonged argument may increase the attention they seek. For abuse, targeted threats or repeated harassment, avoid retaliation, retain relevant messages or screenshots, use the platform's reporting or blocking options and approach a trusted person or appropriate authority when safety is at risk. Bystanders should not forward humiliating material or join in the abuse.

Freedom to disagree is not freedom to harass. The nature of the message, its context and its effect on the recipient matter more than whether the sender calls it a joke.

Prelims focus

  • Real-time chat or a video call is synchronous; email read later is asynchronous.
  • Constructive criticism concerns an idea; personal abuse targets a person.
  • Trolling seeks a disruptive reaction; cyberbullying involves harmful targeting, often repeated.
  • For serious online harassment, preserving evidence and reporting are preferable to retaliation.
  • Trap: Not every disagreement or isolated criticism is cyberbullying.

[NCERT, Computer Science, Class 11, Ch. 11 'Societal Impact', §§11.3.1–11.3.2, pp. 231–233, 2026–27 reprint; CBSE, Digital Citizenship: Level 1 Student Handbook, Grade 6, Lesson 6 'Netiquette'; UNICEF India, 'Stay Safe Online', sections 'Think before you send' and 'Report it!', consulted 5 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Check for repeated abuse or a serious threat first, then provocation; preserve evidence for harm, avoid escalation, and answer disagreement politely.
pictures.caption: A sensible response depends on whether the exchange is a disagreement or harassment.

title: Respectful Communication, Disagreement and Online Harm

body:
What consent means in digital sharing

Consent means permission from the person concerned for a particular action. When a photograph, video, voice recording, screenshot or conversation contains another person's information, the ethical approach is to ask before posting or forwarding it. The fact that the sender possesses a file does not mean that everyone shown in it has agreed to its circulation.

Consent is most meaningful when the person knows what will be shared, with whom and for what purpose, and is free to decline. Permission to take a group photograph is not necessarily permission to post it publicly; permission to send a photograph to a private class group is not automatically permission to repost it on an open social-media account.

Sharing decisions should match the agreed purpose

  1. Identify whose image, voice, message or personal details appear in the material.
  2. Ask the person concerned whether that particular content may be shared with the intended audience.
  3. Check whether the material reveals sensitive information, such as an address, contact number, location, examination document or private conversation.
  4. If permission is absent or the purpose is unclear, do not share; where possible, remove or conceal unnecessary details before seeking renewed permission.

Suppose friends take photographs at a school celebration. One friend agrees to appear in a photograph but asks that it not be placed online. Saving it privately does not authorise publishing it to a public page. A screenshot of a private chat requires the same caution, even if the sender thinks the conversation is amusing.

Consent is not the same as accuracy or attribution

These checks protect different interests. A caption may be completely accurate yet violate privacy because the person did not consent to the disclosure. A photograph may be properly credited to its photographer but still expose a person who did not agree to public sharing. Asking permission from a person appearing in a photograph is also distinct from checking the photographer's rights to the image.

If someone later withdraws their agreement, respect that request and remove content from places under your control where possible. Removal cannot guarantee that copies, downloads or screenshots have disappeared from other people's devices.

Prelims focus

  • Consent concerns permission for a particular use of another person's content or information.
  • Permission to photograph and permission to publish are different.
  • Consent for a private group does not automatically extend to a public post.
  • Accurate content can still be an improper privacy disclosure.
  • Trap: Giving the photographer credit does not substitute for consent from the people affected by the sharing.

[NCERT, Computer Science, Class 11, Ch. 11 'Societal Impact', §11.3.1 'Respect privacy', pp. 231–232, 2026–27 reprint; CBSE and Cyber Peace Foundation, Cyber Safety, 2020, Ch. 3 'Digital Communication', p. 17 ('Posting Photographs' and 'Sharenting'); UNICEF, 'Staying Safe Online', 'Ask before you share someone’s photo or video', consulted 5 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: A group photograph should be shared only with the people concerned in mind.

pictures.alt: Consent to capture differs from consent to share online. Ask about content, use and audience; without permission, stop; with permission, stay within its scope.

title: Consent Before Sharing Photographs, Messages and Recordings

body:
Protecting personal information

Privacy concerns control over access to and use of personal information. Names combined with contact details, home addresses, live location, examination registration details, identity documents, financial records, health information and private photographs may expose a person to avoidable risk when publicly disclosed. Not every item is equally sensitive in every context, but a responsible user shares only what is necessary for a legitimate purpose.

Confidentiality is the duty to avoid disclosing information entrusted to you for a limited purpose, such as a private message or group record. Security refers to protective measures, such as device locks, strong passwords and account access controls. These terms are related but not interchangeable: a securely stored screenshot can still violate confidentiality if its owner publishes it without permission.

Private groups and privacy settings

Limiting a post to selected contacts reduces its ordinary audience, but does not ensure that it cannot be copied, photographed or forwarded. Check who can view posts, contact you and see your location. Do not share other people's login credentials or access their accounts without permission. Be cautious about accepting unknown contacts whose identities have not been established.

Active and passive digital footprints

A digital footprint is a trail of information associated with someone's activity on digital devices or Internet services. It may include information a user intentionally supplies and information generated during normal use.

FootprintHow it arisesExample
ActiveInformation deliberately submittedA public comment, uploaded photograph or completed online form
PassiveData produced during activity, sometimes without the user's deliberate attentionWebsite visit records, cookies or app-use data

The difference concerns how the information is produced, not whether it is harmless or harmful. Both types can affect privacy. Deleting a post may remove it from one visible account, but copies or records could remain elsewhere; permanent removal cannot be assumed.

Privacy settings and deleting posts are useful controls, but neither guarantees complete privacy or erasure. Prevention before disclosure remains important.

Prelims focus

  • Privacy concerns access to personal information; confidentiality concerns protecting entrusted information.
  • Security concerns measures that help prevent unauthorised access.
  • A deliberately uploaded comment creates an active digital footprint.
  • Records generated through website use can form a passive digital footprint.
  • Trap: A private group or deleted message is not proof that no copy survives.

[NCERT, Computer Science, Class 11, Ch. 11 'Societal Impact', §11.2 'Digital Footprints' and §11.4 'Data Protection', pp. 230 and 235, 2026–27 reprint; Indian Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, 'Online Safety Tips', section 'Cyber awareness and hygiene for teens and young adults', consulted 5 November 2026; UNICEF India, 'Stay Safe Online', sections 'Think before you accept' and 'Think before you send', consulted 5 November 2026.]
